title: Noise
summary: Loud noise damages the sensory cells in your ears, and the damage cannot be repaired. Wear the hearing protection your employer provides in high-noise areas and cut your time near loud equipment.
talking_points: Loud noise damages the tiny sensory cells inside your ears. Once damaged, they cannot be repaired. Over time, too much noise causes permanent hearing loss and ringing in the ears (tinnitus).
Noise can also hide warnings and make it hard to understand what people say. Hearing loss can raise the risk of poor health outcomes such as cognitive decline and dementia.
Always wear the hearing protection your employer provides when you are around loud noise. Make sure it works with your other PPE.
Learn how to use hearing protection properly, including how to insert earplugs. Wash your hands before you insert them to help prevent infection.
Try the raised voice test. If you must shout to be heard from 3 feet away (arm's length), wear hearing protection.
Look for caution signs about hazardous noise, check the equipment manual to see if hearing protection is recommended, or ask your supervisor. A smartphone sound level meter app can also help.
Limit your time around loud noise. Take breaks from it, and move away from noise sources or move them away from your work area when possible.
Tell your supervisor if you notice ringing in your ears or muffled hearing at the end of your shift. Get a baseline hearing test early in your career and recheck it regularly.
site_hazards_to_check: Jackhammers, saws, grinders, or other loud tools running where crews cannot talk at arm's length without shouting
Workers in loud areas with no hearing protection, or protection that does not fit with their hard hat or other PPE
Missing or faded caution signs for hazardous noise levels
Loud equipment placed close to where others are working
discussion_questions: Which tools or equipment on this job are loud enough to need hearing protection?
How do you do the raised voice test, and what does it tell you?
What could we do today to make the work area quieter or shorten how long people are exposed?
